title: Many Changes in the Justice Party
translation_notes: Fresh T1 translation was made directly from the pinned Tamil after the complete source review. No pre-existing English translation was consulted as drafting authority.

The first surviving chapter extraction begins only with '-ல்'; the translation restores 'In 1932' because the direct page-42 witness explicitly supplies '1932–ல்'. The reconstruction remains disclosed in the source-note sidecar and does not alter the read-only Tamil JSON.

The source's explicit statement that the Justice Party collapsed in a general election in 1936 is translated as authored. T2/T3 do not silently correct Kalaignar's chronology from external historical summaries.
The page-42/page-43 continuation 'இந்தி எதிர்ப்புக் கிளர்ச்சி!' and the page-44/page-45 Voltaire quotation are reconstructed across extraction boundaries as continuous literary units.
T2 normalises historically attested English forms including Panneerselvam, Khalifullah, Natarajan and Indian National Congress, while retaining Kalaignar's epithets and political framing.

Period office vocabulary is context-sensitive: the 1932 Raja of Bobbili and the earlier P. Subbarayan government use the dyarchy title 'First Minister', while Rajaji's 1937 office is rendered as 'Premier of the Madras Presidency'.
Maraimalai Adigal's 'வடமொழி' is translated as 'Sanskrit', its established lexical sense in this context, rather than the overly literal 'northern language'.
The literary 'இறும்பூது' is rendered as 'wonder'; T2 removes T1's added 'proud' because the word itself does not require that emotional addition.
Rajaji's two-opponents claim and Panneerselvam's numerical reversal remain direct dialogue with the punchline intact.

Maraimalai Adigal's lament, the Thalamuthu-Natarajan blood-and-flag image, the 1938 'this was the year' catalogue, reported criticism of Periyar, and the closing chorus praising Anna retain their rhetorical force rather than being compressed into historical summary.

The anomalous page-45 verb 'நீட்டினார்' is translated only by its secure contextual function: Sami Chidambaranar wrote 'Leader of the Tamils' as a biography of Periyar. No unattested replacement Tamil verb is asserted.
T2 removes the invented nail image from 'ஆணித்தரமான வாதங்கள்' and renders the lexicalised phrase as 'Firm, forceful arguments.'

T3 completed an English-only literary read and accepted 15 minor fluency revisions only after each was rechecked against the pinned Tamil. Deliberately unusual wording carrying Kalaignar's rhetoric was retained.
The thought-structure audit passes 22/22 major movements with no omissions, reordering or invented structural turns; the independent English remains frozen for subsequent terminology/cultural review.
paragraphs: In 1932, a no-confidence resolution was passed against Justice Party leader Munusami Naidu. At the conference convened in Tanjore in connection with it, the Raja of Bobbili took charge as party leader and formally assumed office as First Minister.

Though this ministry was meant to last only three years, delay in the publication of the Simon Commission's report stretched the life of the ministry to seven years. During that period, the Raja of Chettinad, Muthiah Chettiar, and the Gold of Tanjore, the Lion of Tamil, Sir A. T. Panneerselvam, also took office as ministers.

In the general election held in 1936 under the reforms that followed the Simon Commission's report, the Justice Party suffered a complete collapse. That very year, I was in the Fifth Standard at high school, having learnt the history of the Raja of Panagal backwards and forwards and earning my teacher's praise.

It was in 1937 that a Congress ministry first assumed office in the Madras Presidency. Because the Congress Party took part directly in this general election, the Swaraj Party disappeared. The Congress ministry was formed with Rajaji as Premier.

As soon as Rajaji became Premier of the Madras Presidency, he made Hindi a compulsory subject in the schools. As soon as the law making Hindi compulsory was enacted, lovers of Tamil and eminent scholars, who had already foreseen it and been expressing their opposition, rose with vigour. They organized agitations. They passed resolutions declaring that Hindi was not wanted and sent them to the government. Through the newspapers they poured forth condemnations that rose like a red flame. In the cities of Tamil Nadu, in hamlets and tiny villages—everywhere, anti-Hindi agitation!

Confronted by this opposition, Rajaji began to impose Hindi still more forcefully. Even the Tamils within the Congress did not, at heart, favour compulsory Hindi. A good example was Navalar Somasundara Bharathiar, who left the Congress and began to raise a lion's roar against Hindi.
Speaking in the legislature, Rajaji said, 'Who are the people opposing Hindi? Only two! One is Ramasami Naicker; the other is Pasumalai Bharathiar.'

Panneerselvam, seated on the opposition benches, immediately rose and replied, 'There are two opposing it. But you are the one person bringing Hindi in. Therefore the majority is on the side of opposition.' Hearing that reply, all Tamil Nadu praised Panneerselvam and rejoiced.

Maraimalai Adigal of Pallavaram—the gracious speaker of classical Tamil—also plunged into the anti-Hindi struggle. 'Alas! Sanskrit has come and brought Tamil so low! English has left it barely alive! If Hindi comes now, Tamil's destruction is certain. Ayyo! What shall we do?' he lamented. For Maraimalai Adigal, who lamented thus, the anti-Hindi movement brought great consolation.

On 3 June 1938, Maraimalai Adigal presided over the anti-Hindi conference held at Saidapet. Yes! When I think again and again that on June 3—the very day on which I was born—Maraimalai Adigal presided over a conference that rallied and roused the people for the first battle against Hindi to protect Tamil, I am filled with wonder.

Periyar led the anti-Hindi war that began in 1938. Arignar Anna, Muthamizh Kaavalar K. A. P. Viswanatham, Navalar Somasundara Bharathiar, Moovalur Ramamirtham Ammaiyar, along with eminent poets and Tamil savants, stood arrayed in the front ranks of the anti-Hindi force.

Pickets were held at the gates of schools where Hindi had been made compulsory, and more than a thousand men and women went to prison. Two Tamil heroes, Thalamuthu and Natarajan, went to prison opposing Hindi and became corpses within the prison walls. The Tamil dipped the flag of his language struggle in the blood of those heroes and sent it flying until it touched the sky.
Fourteen years lay between 1924 and 1938. At school I had reached the Second Form. How many, how many events had taken place in the country during those years!

It was in 1938 that Subhas Chandra Bose was elected president of the Indian National Congress. As soon as he was elected, Pandit Nehru went to Europe to rest. Nehru was not in India for that whole year!

Dr Subbarayan, who had governed the Madras Presidency as First Minister with the support of the Justice Party, was Education Minister in Rajaji's ministry in 1938. It was in his room, on 25 February 1938, that the decision was taken to make Hindi a compulsory subject in Tamil Nadu.

Just two days later, on February 27, at Kanchipuram, Khan Bahadur Khalifullah Sahib, M.L.A., raised the flag of anti-Hindi resistance in Tamil Nadu. It was at this conference that Somasundara Bharathiar raised his voice against Hindi. It was also at this conference that Periyar unveiled the portrait of the Revolutionary Poet Bharathidasan.

A resolution was moved at the conference: 'Public money in the government budget must not be spent on the unnecessary Hindi language.' Tamilavel Uma Maheswaran Pillai and Chidambaram N. Dandapani thundered in support of the resolution.
Do you know who moved that resolution? It was Perarignar Anna! In those days: C. N. Annadurai, M.A.

It was in this very year, when Tamil Nadu had become a battlefield in the language struggle, that Kemal Pasha died in Turkey! It was the year Hitler swallowed Czechoslovakia—the year the first step toward the Second World War was taken. It was also the year Stalin was carrying out a great purge in Russia and sending thousands of people to Siberia and elsewhere. It was the time when Gandhiji's principles of non-violence were locked in fierce conflict with the policies of Congress president Subhas Bose!

As Voltaire said, 'I cannot agree, letter for letter, with what you say. But I will fight, giving even my life, so that the views you have the courage to express are not obstructed in any way.' In the same way, it was a year when Subhas Chandra Bose agreed with nothing Gandhiji said, yet opposed with fierce intensity anything he saw as harming Gandhi's welfare, fame, service or honour!

Non-violence—democracy—individual rights—self-government—secure frontiers—the pride of race—the preciousness of the mother tongue—honest politics: it was a year when all these, throughout the world, came under severe challenge!

Countless views were expressed about Periyar's leadership of the anti-Hindi war. 'He has no intention of opposing Hindi for the growth and advancement of Tamil. He has no concern for Tamils. He has made the anti-Hindi agitation a weapon for fulfilling his fervent aim of destroying the Congress,' it was written. It was said.

Periyar, who had become the leader of the anti-Hindi struggle, came to be accepted in that period as the Leader of the Tamils. The learned Sami Chidambaranar wrote the substantial book 'Leader of the Tamils' as a biography of Periyar.
In the anti-Hindi campaign, a new name—Annadurai—began to echo through every nook and corner of Tamil Nadu.
'How the man speaks!'
'It feels like listening to music!'
'No dance, no song, hardly a movement—he turns slowly on the stage and scatters Tamil words like pomegranate pearls!'
'What simile! What beauty!'
'Short in stature! A guileless gaze! Speech like a sluice gate flung open!'
'Firm, forceful arguments. Statistics no one can deny. Ah! Is that speech? The Courtallam waterfall! A lilting Tamil chindu!'
Praise like this for his speeches poured in from the educated and from ordinary people alike.
